notes:
Principal value branches

FunctionDomainRange (principal branch)
$\sin^{-1}x$$[-1,1]$$[-\pi/2,\pi/2]$
$\cos^{-1}x$$[-1,1]$$[0,\pi]$
$\tan^{-1}x$$\mathbb{R}$$(-\pi/2,\pi/2)$
$\csc^{-1}x$$|x|\ge1$$[-\pi/2,\pi/2]-\{0\}$
$\sec^{-1}x$$|x|\ge1$$[0,\pi]-\{\pi/2\}$
$\cot^{-1}x$$\mathbb{R}$$(0,\pi)$

Key identities

  • $\sin^{-1}x+\cos^{-1}x=\pi/2$; $\tan^{-1}x+\cot^{-1}x=\pi/2$; $\sec^{-1}x+\csc^{-1}x=\pi/2$ (each for $x$ in the respective domain).
  • $\sin^{-1}(-x)=-\sin^{-1}x$, $\tan^{-1}(-x)=-\tan^{-1}x$ (odd); $\cos^{-1}(-x)=\pi-\cos^{-1}x$, $\cot^{-1}(-x)=\pi-\cot^{-1}x$, $\sec^{-1}(-x)=\pi-\sec^{-1}x$.
  • $\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac1x\right)=\csc^{-1}x$ for $|x|\ge1$; similarly $\cos^{-1}(1/x)=\sec^{-1}x$, $\tan^{-1}(1/x)=\cot^{-1}x$ for $x>0$ (add $\pi$ adjustments for $x<0$ where relevant).

Sum/difference formulas

  • $\tan^{-1}x+\tan^{-1}y=\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{x+y}{1-xy}\right)$, valid when $xy<1$; add/subtract $\pi$ when $xy>1$ depending on sign of $x,y$.
  • $2\tan^{-1}x=\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{2x}{1+x^2}\right)=\cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1-x^2}{1+x^2}\right)=\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{2x}{1-x^2}\right)$ for $|x|\le1$ (first form) or as appropriate.
  • Substitution tricks: for $\sqrt{1-x^2}$ put $x=\sin\theta$; for $\sqrt{1+x^2}$ put $x=\tan\theta$; for $\sqrt{x^2-1}$ put $x=\sec\theta$.

Common values

  • $\sin^{-1}(1/2)=\pi/6$, $\sin^{-1}(1/\sqrt2)=\pi/4$, $\sin^{-1}(\sqrt3/2)=\pi/3$, $\sin^{-1}(1)=\pi/2$.
  • $\tan^{-1}(1)=\pi/4$, $\tan^{-1}(\sqrt3)=\pi/3$, $\tan^{-1}(1/\sqrt3)=\pi/6$.

Exam tip

KCET typically sets 1-2 questions from this chapter, mostly direct evaluation of a principal value or a two-term $\tan^{-1}$/$\sin^{-1}$ addition formula. Memorise the range tables carefully — a common trap is using the wrong principal branch for $\cos^{-1}$ or $\cot^{-1}$ of a negative number.

questions.explanation: $\sin(\pi/6)=1/2$ and $\pi/6\in[-\pi/2,\pi/2]$, so it is the principal value.
questions.trick: Recall standard triangle values: $\sin(\pi/6)=1/2$.

questions.explanation: $\cos^{-1}(-x)=\pi-\cos^{-1}x=\pi-\pi/3=2\pi/3$, which lies in $[0,\pi]$.
questions.trick: $\cos^{-1}(-x)=\pi-\cos^{-1}x$ for negative inputs.
Combine two terms with the $\tan^{-1}$ addition formula first, then add the rest.

questions.explanation: This is a standard identity valid for all $x\in[-1,1]$.
questions.trick: $\sin^{-1}x+\cos^{-1}x=\pi/2$ always — instant answer, no computation.

questions.explanation: Let $\theta=\sin^{-1}(3/5)$, so $\sin\theta=3/5$ and $\theta$ is in the first quadrant. Then $\cos\theta=\sqrt{1-9/25}=4/5$.
questions.trick: Draw the 3-4-5 triangle: $\sin\theta=3/5\Rightarrow\cos\theta=4/5$.

questions.explanation: $\sec\theta$ never takes values strictly between $-1$ and $1$, so its inverse is defined only for $|x|\ge1$.
questions.trick: $\sec\theta$ never lies strictly between $-1$ and $1$, so domain is $|x|\ge1$.

questions.explanation: $\tan^{-1}$ is an odd function: $\tan^{-1}(-1)=-\tan^{-1}(1)=-\pi/4$, which lies in $(-\pi/2,\pi/2)$.

questions.trick: Convert $\cot^{-1}(-x)=\pi-\cot^{-1}x$, then just subtract standard angles.
$2\tan^{-1}x=\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{2x}{1-x^2}\right)$ for $|x|<1$.

questions.explanation: $\sin^{-1}(-1/2)=-\pi/6$, so expression $=\sin(\pi/3+\pi/6)=\sin(\pi/2)=1$.
questions.trick: Evaluate the inner inverse first, then simply add the angles.
Take cosine of both sides: $x=\cos(\pi/6)$.

questions.q: The range of the principal branch of $\cot^{-1}x$ is
questions.explanation: The principal branch of $\cot^{-1}x$ is taken as $(0,\pi)$, excluding the endpoints since $\cot$ is undefined there in the usual convention.
questions.trick: $\cot^{-1}$ principal range is the open interval $(0,\pi)$.

questions.explanation: Let $\theta=\cos^{-1}(4/5)$, so $\cos\theta=4/5$, $\sin\theta=3/5$ (first quadrant), hence $\tan\theta=3/4$.
questions.trick: 3-4-5 triangle again: $\cos\theta=4/5\Rightarrow\tan\theta=3/4$.

questions.explanation: $3\pi/4$ is outside $[-\pi/2,\pi/2]$. $\sin(3\pi/4)=\sin(\pi/4)$, and $\pi/4$ lies in the principal range, so the answer is $\pi/4$.
questions.trick: Use $\sin(\pi-x)=\sin x$ to pull the angle into $[-\pi/2,\pi/2]$ first.

questions.explanation: $7\pi/6$ is outside $[0,\pi]$. $\cos(7\pi/6)=\cos(2\pi-7\pi/6)=\cos(5\pi/6)$ since cosine is even about $2\pi$; actually $\cos(7\pi/6)=-\cos(\pi/6)=\cos(\pi-\pi/6)=\cos(5\pi/6)$, and $5\pi/6\in[0,\pi]$, so the answer is $5\pi/6$.
questions.trick: Reduce the angle into $[0,\pi]$ using cosine symmetry before reading it off.

questions.explanation: $\tan(\pi/4)=\dfrac{x+y}{1-xy}=1\Rightarrow x+y=1-xy\Rightarrow x+y+xy=1$.
questions.trick: $\tan(\text{sum})=1\Rightarrow(x+y)/(1-xy)=1$ gives $x+y+xy$ directly.

questions.explanation: $\csc(\pi/6)=1/\sin(\pi/6)=1/(1/2)=2$, and $\pi/6$ lies in the principal range.
questions.trick: $\csc\theta=2\Rightarrow\sin\theta=1/2\Rightarrow\theta=\pi/6$.

questions.explanation: Using $\sin^{-1}x+\sin^{-1}y=\sin^{-1}(x\sqrt{1-y^2}+y\sqrt{1-x^2})$: $=\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{4}{5}\cdot\dfrac{12}{13}+\dfrac{5}{13}\cdot\dfrac{3}{5}\right)=\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{48+15}{65}\right)=\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{63}{65}\right)$.
By definition $\cot\theta=1/7$, so $\tan\theta=1/\cot\theta=7$.
questions.trick: $\tan\theta=1/\cot\theta$ — just flip the given fraction.

questions.explanation: $\sin\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)=-\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ and $-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\in\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$, so it is the principal value.
questions.trick: Odd function: $\sin^{-1}(-x)=-\sin^{-1}x$, then use a standard angle.

questions.explanation: Using $\tan^{-1}x+\cot^{-1}x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ for all real $x$, the sum is $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.
questions.trick: $\tan^{-1}x+\cot^{-1}x=\pi/2$ for any real $x$.

questions.explanation: We need $-1\le 2x-1\le 1 \Rightarrow 0\le 2x\le 2 \Rightarrow 0\le x\le 1$, so the domain is $[0,1]$.
questions.trick: Set $-1\le(\text{inner expression})\le1$ and solve for $x$.

questions.explanation: Since $\sin^{-1}x+\cos^{-1}x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, the sum equals $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, and $\cos\dfrac{\pi}{2}=0$.
questions.trick: The sum inside is $\pi/2$ by identity, so $\cos(\pi/2)=0$.

questions.explanation: Let $\sin^{-1}\dfrac{3}{5}=\theta$, so $\sin\theta=\dfrac{3}{5},\cos\theta=\dfrac{4}{5}$. Then $\sin2\theta=2\sin\theta\cos\theta=2\cdot\dfrac35\cdot\dfrac45=\dfrac{24}{25}$.
questions.trick: Find $\sin\theta,\cos\theta$ from a triangle, then use $\sin2\theta=2\sin\theta\cos\theta$.

questions.explanation: Since $2\times3=6>1$, use $\tan^{-1}x+\tan^{-1}y=\pi+\tan^{-1}\dfrac{x+y}{1-xy}$ for $x,y>0,xy>1$: $\tan^{-1}\dfrac{5}{1-6}=\tan^{-1}(-1)=-\dfrac{\pi}{4}$, so the sum is $\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{4}=\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$.
questions.trick: Both positive with $xy>1$ $\Rightarrow$ add $\pi$ to the addition-formula result.

questions.q: The range of the principal branch of $\sec^{-1}x$ is
questions.explanation: The principal branch of $\sec^{-1}x$ has range $[0,\pi]$ excluding $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ (where secant is undefined).
questions.trick: $\sec^{-1}$ range is $[0,\pi]$ minus the undefined point $\pi/2$.

questions.q: Which of the following is INCORRECT?
questions.explanation: $\cos^{-1}$ is not an odd function; the correct identity is $\cos^{-1}(-x)=\pi-\cos^{-1}x$, so option D is false.
questions.trick: Only $\cos^{-1}$, $\cot^{-1}$, $\sec^{-1}$ are non-odd — check the sign rule per function.

questions.explanation: Principal range of $\cot^{-1}$ is $(0,\pi)$. Since $\cot\dfrac{2\pi}{3}=-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}$, the value is $\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$.
questions.trick: Use $\pi-\cot^{-1}(1/\sqrt3)$ since $\cot^{-1}$'s range is $(0,\pi)$.

questions.explanation: $\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$ is outside $\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$, but $\sin\dfrac{5\pi}{6}=\sin\left(\pi-\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\right)=\sin\dfrac{\pi}{6}$, and $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ lies in the principal range, so the answer is $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$.
questions.trick: $\sin(\pi-x)=\sin x$: reduce $5\pi/6$ down to $\pi/6$ inside the range.

questions.explanation: Using the sum formula, $\tan^{-1}\dfrac{\frac{x-1}{x-2}+\frac{x+1}{x+2}}{1-\frac{(x-1)(x+1)}{(x-2)(x+2)}}=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$. Simplifying the numerator and denominator and solving gives $2x^2=1$, so $x=\pm\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$.
questions.trick: Apply the $\tan^{-1}$ addition formula, set result $=\tan(\pi/4)=1$, solve.

questions.explanation: \(\cos^{-1}\dfrac12=\dfrac{\pi}{3}\) and \(\sin^{-1}\dfrac12=\dfrac{\pi}{6}\), so the sum is \(\dfrac{\pi}{3}+2\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{6}=\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\).
questions.trick: Recall standard values $\pi/3$ and $\pi/6$, then combine with the given coefficients.
Convert each term to $\tan^{-1}$ form via a triangle, then apply $\tan(A+B)$.

questions.q: The graph of $y=\tan^{-1}x$ has which of the following properties?
options: It is bounded between $-\pi$ and $\pi$ and is decreasing
It has horizontal asymptotes at $y=\pm\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ and is increasing
questions.explanation: $\tan^{-1}x$ is strictly increasing on $\mathbb{R}$ with $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to\pm\infty}\tan^{-1}x=\pm\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, giving horizontal asymptotes $y=\pm\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.
questions.trick: $\tan^{-1}x$ is increasing with horizontal asymptotes $y=\pm\pi/2$, no vertical ones.

questions.explanation: Since $\theta\in\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$, $\cos\theta\ge0$, so $\cos\theta=\sqrt{1-\sin^2\theta}=\sqrt{1-x^2}$.
questions.trick: $\theta\in[-\pi/2,\pi/2]\Rightarrow\cos\theta\ge0$, so take the $+$ square root.

questions.explanation: $2\tan^{-1}\frac13=\tan^{-1}\dfrac{2\cdot\frac13}{1-\frac19}=\tan^{-1}\dfrac{2/3}{8/9}=\tan^{-1}\dfrac{3}{4}$. Then $\tan^{-1}\frac34+\tan^{-1}\frac17=\tan^{-1}\dfrac{\frac34+\frac17}{1-\frac34\cdot\frac17}=\tan^{-1}\dfrac{\frac{25}{28}}{\frac{25}{28}}=\tan^{-1}(1)=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$.
questions.trick: Combine the first pair with the double-angle formula, then add the last term.

questions.q: Assertion (A): $\sin^{-1}(\sin 4)$ is not equal to $4$. Reason (R): $4$ radians does not lie in $\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, R is false
A is false, R is true
questions.explanation: Since $\pi\approx3.14<4<\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\approx4.71$, the value $4$ lies outside $\left[-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right]$, hence $\sin^{-1}(\sin4)\ne4$; R correctly explains why A is true.
questions.trick: Reduce the angle into the principal range before equating to the raw input value.

questions.explanation: $\sec\dfrac{\pi}{6}=\dfrac{1}{\cos(\pi/6)}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3/2}=\dfrac{2}{\sqrt3}$, and $\dfrac{\pi}{6}\in[0,\pi]-\{\pi/2\}$, so it is the principal value.
questions.trick: $\sec\theta=2/\sqrt3\Rightarrow\cos\theta=\sqrt3/2\Rightarrow\theta=\pi/6$.

questions.explanation: If $x=y$, then $2\cos^{-1}x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\Rightarrow\cos^{-1}x=\dfrac{\pi}{4}\Rightarrow x=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$. So $x^2+y^2=\dfrac12+\dfrac12=1$.
questions.trick: Equal angles: each is $\pi/4$, then square and add both values.

questions.q: Which of the following pairs (function, domain) is INCORRECT?
questions.explanation: $\csc^{-1}x$ is defined for $|x|\ge1$, i.e. domain $\mathbb{R}-(-1,1)$, not $[-1,1]$ — so option C is incorrect.
questions.trick: $\csc^{-1}x$ excludes $(-1,1)$; its domain is $|x|\ge1$, not $[-1,1]$.
